Tesla says battery supply, not demand, is what’s holding back its car sales. In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, the automaker wrote that “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter.”
It also claims it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.” But the numbers in the same letter don’t line up with a company that has more buyers than cars.
Tesla’s new explanation for flat sales
The battery line has been building for a while. In Q2, Tesla called battery pack capacity “the main limiting factor to near-term vehicle production volume increase.” Now it says batteries limited what it could sell during the quarter itself.
Tesla didn’t put a number on the backlog. It did list record deliveries in Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan, and record production at Gigafactory Berlin. Elsewhere in the Q3 2026 financial results , Tesla says it is focused on “increasing production across our factories” because of “strong demand.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
What Tesla’s own numbers show
Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3 , down 2% from 497,099 a year ago. Model 3 and Model Y were down 1%. “Other models,” which covers Cybertruck, Semi and what’s left of Model S and X, fell 48% to 8,295 units.
It built 464,391 vehicles, so it delivered 22,141 more than it produced. That’s the second quarter in a row Tesla has worked down inventory, after building about 50,000 more cars than it sold in Q1. Global inventory fell to 11 days of supply, from 27 days in Q1 and 15 in Q2.
Model 3 and Model Y production ran at about 1.83 million units annualized. Tesla lists more than 2.25 million units of installed capacity for those two models across Fremont, Shanghai, Berlin and Texas. So the factories ran at roughly 81%.
And here’s the part that doesn’t fit. In its list of reasons revenue didn’t grow, Tesla cited “lower vehicle average selling price (ASP)” year-over-year, even after excluding currency effects. Automakers that can’t build cars fast enough usually raise prices, or at least stop discounting.
Where Tesla’s batteries are going
Tesla has more places to put battery cells than it used to. The same letter says energy storage had its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and Tesla is increasing 4680 cell output “to support the ramps of both Cybercab and Tesla Semi along with higher Model Y volumes.”
Tesla’s outlook even says deliveries depend on “allocation decisions between sale to customers and use for our owned and operated fleet.” So part of the battery constraint is Tesla deciding where its cells go.
Electrek’s Take
Battery supply is a real issue, and tariffs on Chinese cells make it harder in the US. Tesla also did set records in a few markets, but overall deliveries are down, and Tesla is selling cars for lower than it used to. Those are not signs of a company that is supply constrained.
In fact, today, in 2026, Tesla has more battery suppliers than ever, and it has itself ramped up production of its own battery cells.
But “we’re supply constrained” is one of Tesla’s oldest lines, and this letter doesn’t prove it. Deliveries fell year-over-year. Prices fell. Two quarters ago, Tesla built 50,000 cars it couldn’t sell. If batteries were really the bottleneck, Tesla would be raising prices and keeping the extra margin, not lowering ASPs.
The more likely answer is that it’s a bit of both. Demand recovered somewhat in some markets, and Tesla is choosing to send more cells to Megapack, Cybercab and Semi because it thinks those businesses are worth more. That’s a reasonable strategy. It’s just not the same as having more customers than it can serve.

Tesla (TSLA) released its financial results and shareholders’ letter for the third quarter (Q3) 2026 after market close today. We’re updating this post with all the details from the financial results, shareholders’ letter, and the conference call later tonight.
The earnings call with management is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. ET.
Tesla Q3 2026 earnings expectations
Wall Street came into the report expecting a flat quarter. The FactSet consensus, as displayed on Estimize, called for $28.06 billion in revenue, essentially unchanged from the $28.1 billion Tesla posted in Q3 2025 and a bit below the $28.24 billion it reported last quarter.
Profit expectations were lower. Analysts were looking for non-GAAP earnings of $0.45 per share, down 10% from $0.50 a year ago. The Estimize crowd was slightly more bullish at $28.36 billion and $0.48.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
We already had the volume numbers. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3 , down 2.1% year-over-year but well ahead of the 461,974 consensus, while producing only 464,391. It also deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago but short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected. For the full setup, see our Q3 2026 earnings preview .
So the question was never volume. It was whether Tesla could stop the profit slide after Q2, when operating margin fell to 1.4% and EPS missed the consensus by 20 cents.
Tesla Q3 2026 financial results
After the market closed today, Tesla released its financial results for the third quarter and reported $28.05 billion in revenue, flat from a year ago and in line with the $28.06 billion Wall Street expected. Non-GAAP earnings came in at $0.48 per share, beating the $0.45 consensus but down 4% from $0.50 a year ago.
It’s a better quarter than Q2, but the trend hasn’t changed. Margins recovered, with auto gross margin excluding credits back above 18%, yet operating income still fell 56% year-over-year as spending on AI and Optimus grew faster than gross profit. On a GAAP basis, net income dropped 43% to $787 million, or $0.22 per share.
Total gross margin was 19.6%, up 160 basis points from 18.0% a year ago and well above the 16.8% Tesla posted in Q2. Operating income fell 56% to $718 million, for an operating margin of 2.6%, compared with 5.8% a year ago and 1.4% last quarter.
Operating expenses came in at $4.78 billion, up 39% year-over-year. Research and development alone jumped 69% to $2.76 billion as Tesla spends on what it now calls “Super Intelligence” (SI), Optimus, and the Cybercab. Stock-based compensation, which includes the 2025 CEO pay package, hit $1.17 billion, up from $663 million a year ago.
Capital spending was $4.73 billion, more than double the $2.25 billion of a year ago, and free cash flow came in at $1.53 billion, compared with $3.99 billion a year ago and negative $1.09 billion in Q2. Tesla ended the quarter with $45.4 billion in cash and investments. GAAP net income included a $288 million unrealized gain on Tesla’s bitcoin holdings, partly offset by a $142 million unrealized loss on its SpaceX equity investment.
That puts Tesla’s capex at $13.01 billion through the first nine months of 2026, only about half of the “more than $25 billion” management guided for the year. To hit that number, Tesla would need to spend roughly $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter so far. The Q3 letter doesn’t update the guidance, and capex actually fell sequentially from $5.79 billion in Q2. So either Q4 spending explodes, or the 2026 plan is quietly slipping into 2027. The lower spending also flatters this quarter’s positive free cash flow.

Tesla’s auto margin without credits
The number we watch first is automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits, now that the credit market has mostly dried up. It came in at 18.1% this quarter, up from 16.3% in Q2 and 15.4% a year ago, though still below the 19.2% of Q1, when Tesla got help from warranty and tariff one-time benefits. Tesla credits a better regional and product mix and more FSD subscription revenue, partly offset by lower average selling prices.
Regulatory credits brought in just $113 million, down 73% from $417 million a year ago and below the $146 million in Q2. That line isn’t coming back now that automakers no longer pay federal fuel-economy penalties.
Energy was the weak spot on revenue. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion, which Tesla partly blames on tariff-related customer refunds, even though deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh. The segment’s gross margin jumped to 33% from 20% in Q2, but energy gross profit still slipped to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago.
Services and other was the bright spot. Revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion, and Tesla says gross profit hit a record $734 million on charging, insurance and parts sales.
Tesla blames batteries, not demand
Tesla says “battery availability continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter,” and that it ended Q3 with “the largest backlog for our passenger vehicles in four years.”
That’s a new explanation for flat sales. Deliveries were still down 2% year-over-year, “other models” (Cybertruck, Semi, Model S and X) fell 48%, and Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it built, bringing inventory down to 11 days of supply from 15 in Q2. But average selling prices fell again, which isn’t usually what a supply-constrained automaker does.
On autonomy, Tesla says active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, as defined in Musk’s 2025 pay package. Its Robotaxi service reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by the end of the quarter, a month after Cybercab joined the Austin fleet.

Cars start losing value the moment they are driven off the showroom floor. This is something that surprises owners every time. It was the case for this Chevy Corvette Stingray owner as well. He bought the car in April, drove 700 miles, listed it for sale, but the ‘Vette failed to reach the reserve, so he is now stuck with it.
The car in question is a 2026 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray Coupe 2LT, finished in Blade Silver Metallic over a Sky Cool Gray leather interior, sheltered by a removable roof panel, and riding on alloy wheels measuring 19 inches up front and 20 inches out back.
The driver and passenger sit in heated and ventilated seats with yellow seat belts. The driver gets the relevant driving data via the head-up display and can record track performance with the help of the performance data and video recorder. A Bose sound system provides the soundtrack when the driver has had enough of the V8 orchestra.
Speaking of which, the 6.2-liter LT2 V8 with naturally aspirated firepower pumps out 495 horsepower (502 metric horsepower) when the Z51 package is involved, which is not the case for this car, so it sticks to 490 horsepower (497 metric horsepower) and 470 pound-feet (637 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Cars and Bids Those are enough to make the car rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 2.9 seconds, run the quarter mile in 11.2 seconds, and top out at 194 mph (312 kph). A dual-clutch eight-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion.
However, the owner did not enjoy much of those. He bought the Chevrolet Corvette Stingray back in April, drove just 686 miles (1,104 kilometers), and listed it for sale. It’s usually either incompatibility, having another car on the way, or the Mrs. telling the Mr. to get rid of it ASAP.
However, the market decides how soon because the first attempt at selling it gloriously failed. The original owner paid $83,965 to go home with it six months ago and listed it for sale for an undisclosed reserve. Bidding stopped at $61,000, and the owner is stuck with the car for the moment.
Not even the clean Carfax report with no mileage discrepancies and no accidents convinced bidders to offer more. Better luck next time. But as time passes, the only way for the value of a car is down, unless it is a rare collectable model, which is not the case.
Besides, this 2026 Chevy Corvette Stingray is lacking three important features: the very sought-after Z51 package, the front lift, and the Magnetic Ride Control. With the seller failing to answer the questions of those interested in the car, no wonder he still has it in his garage.

Photo: Ford
Ford came up with a new way to sell Bronco customers the aftermarket through dealers. The ORV Package has just landed in the Ford Custom Garage catalog as a dealer-installed option, stacking a lot of stuff that makes a world of difference off the beaten path. Said package retails at $18,995 and is compatible with three models: four-door Base, Big Bend, and the Outer Banks.
From the standpoint of capability, the biggest upgrade over the four-door Base, Big Bend, and Outer Banks is FOX off-road suspension. Not only does it tighten damping and improve articulation, but additional ground clearance is a must for off-roading shenanigans. The package further transplants the Raptor's front and fuel tank plates, belly armor that said trims have never carried.
Rocker panel trail armor guards the sills on trails that tend to bite, whereas the modular front bumper pulls off the trick certain aftermarket bumpers do not manage. Specifically, the Ford -designed modular bumper keeps all sensors functional. RIGID auxiliary lighting tucks into that bumper. An auxiliary switch kit runs them, plus whatever powered gadget may come next.
The included ProCal tool is there for loading custom calibrations, with said tool doubling as a data logger. Matte-black WELD alloy wheels are in the offing as well, measuring 17 by 8.5 inches at every corner. These alloys ship with black lug nuts and no rubber, which means that customers have to source 315/70 R17 tires.
Otherwise put, the package will set you back more than $18,995. And that's before dealer pricing and installation charges. The rest of the package is all about identity, beginning with red tow hooks, Havoc fender flares, and red grille lettering. A stealth hood decal and a smoked Ford oval are featured as well.
Photo: Ford The visual treatment continues with a black tailgate badge and ORV fender badging. As implied, ORV stands for off-road vehicle. All components carry a supplemental three-year warranty honored at any Ford dealer nationwide. Bolting the kit does not void the factory coverage. Better still, any dealer or ASE-certified tech can do the install without touching the standard warranties.
As you may remember, Ford previewed this package as a concept at the 202 SEMA Show in Las Vegas. Less than a year to mature from a concept into a catalog item is pretty sweet, and that's not all. Optional extras include an ARB air compressor, a hydraulic hood lift kit, and a Borla high-clearance exhaust.
A heavy-duty rear diff cover is also available, as are Ford Performance sill plates and RIGID pods for the hood and roof. As of this writing, the ORV Package is described as a limited edition by its maker. Ford hasn't said how many will be produced for the US market.
It's not clear whether an ORV Package is coming for the 2027 model year Bronco as well. Instead of the familiar 2.7-liter EcoBoost V6, the 2027 levels up to the 3.0-liter EcoBoost V6 . In addition to the Bronco, the 2.7 is gone from the Ranger and F-150 as well.

Between us, Acura’s current lineup feels a bit old and quite unexciting, as it includes models such as the ADX, RDX, and MDX crossovers, as well as the Integra, so there is definitely room for improvement. But is the company actually planning such a thing?
If you had asked us a couple of weeks ago, then we would have told you that “maybe” is the word that answers this question best. After all, we all heard rumors about a possible expansion to include a few novelties, haven’t we? Well, fast forward to a few days ago, and we have official confirmation that Acura is indeed planning to release more models. More particularly, there will be two of them, and these rides will be quite different, not only from each other, but also from other vehicles that the automaker currently has in its portfolio.
So, what are we talking about exactly? Well, the one that America is definitely waiting for more is the new flagship SUV . This will be the biggest high-rider that the company has ever made, and it will be offered with three rows of seats, and seating for up to eight. Chances are higher specs might get individual captain’s chairs for the second and third rows, so they will probably be six seaters. However, you may want to refrain from quoting us on this information, because it is just our two cents, and should be taken with a pinch of salt.
What we can confirm, however, is that this model is indeed coming. Acura recently made the big announcement, some two months after a report spoke about this model. The vehicle is currently known as the Acura XL, and this is the codename, as no one who is not directly involved in its development knows what it will be christened. And that’s not all, because details about it are also unknown. Thus, we cannot tell you anything about the size, equipment, powertrain family, and even the underpinnings.
Photo: Kolesa You see, Acura has not confirmed whether this model will be entirely new, based on a fresh construction, or whether it will share its nuts and bolts with other existing models. The Acura XL will sit above the seven-seat MDX , and it will likely have plenty of things in common with the Honda Pilot XXL (unofficial name) that is also in the making as we speak. The latter will be bigger than the Grand Highlander. And we also have no idea when it will officially debut, though reports speak about a possible launch in 2029.
Thus, we are still a few good years away from seeing the so-called Acura XL, and by then, a lot of things could change. But what exactly is the second model that Acura is planning? Well, it is an “adventure-ready” SUV. The company described it by using words such as “modern,” “premium styling,” “comfort,” and so on. And just like the XL, we also do not know whether it will be based on an existing crossover or not, though some believe that the Passport could be a great foundation.
Now, we may not know anything about this model at this point, though that hasn’t stopped Kolesa’ pixel master, Nikita Chuyko, from imagining it. The images shared in the gallery are nothing more than mere renderings. And if you believe that the design is quite familiar, that’s because the car in question has been based on the Honda Passport TrailSport . Compared to its more mainstream sibling, it features a new front fascia that is clearly Acura. The headlights, grille, bumper, hood, and front fenders are entirely new.
Photo: Kolesa The profile, on the other hand, carries over from the Passport TrailSport, complete with the black plastic cladding on the lower parts of the body. The wheels are bigger, and they are the same ones from the official teaser that Acura recently released. The door handles, side mirrors, roof rails, and so on, carry over from the Honda. Out back, we can see a completely different lighting signature, as well as a new bumper, and a redesigned tailgate.
A look inside hasn’t been provided in this case, though the interior should be very similar to that of the Honda Passport TrailSport . However, in order to set them apart, we reckon that such a thing would feature different screens, as well as a more premium setup overall, and probably a few other tweaks. But let’s not forget that we do not really know whether Acura’s “adventure-ready” SUV will indeed share its underpinnings with the Honda mentioned above, and even if it does, chances are it won’t look anything like this.
The adventurous, high-riding Acura will launch in the first half of 2028, and additional details about it will be released in due course. Meanwhile, feel free to tell us whether you dig the styling of this rendered SUV. So, do you?

BYD is set to launch the Denza N8 EV next week, a large five-seat luxury electric SUV with a CLTC range of over 623 miles (1,000 km).
BYD Denza N8 EV launches on October 26
The Denza N8 initially went on sale in China in 2023 as a mid-to-large-size luxury SUV. It was available as a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) with six- and seven-seat configurations.
BYD is preparing to introduce an all-electric version that will deliver the same electric-only driving range as the PHEV did on a full charge and full tank of gas, combined.
“The king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza calls it, will use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging Technology. The setup delivers “a world-leading 1,003 km pure electric range,” under CLTC conditions, Denza claimed.

BYD’s 1,500 kW Flash Charging tech powers compatible vehicles from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes.
According to a regulatory filing released by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in August, the Denza N8 EV is 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase.
The Denza N8 EV will use a massive 130.15 kWh battery, providing a pure electric CLTC range of up to 623 miles (1,003 km).
BYD will offer a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).
The tri-motor Denza N8, meanwhile, is based on BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, delivering a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).
Denza N8 interior (Source: Denza)
Inside, the luxury SUV features two huge digital screens. One 30″ center infotainment screen spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, and a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) sits below the windshield.
Like many new BYD models, the cabin adopts a minimalist design with premium features like ambient lighting, a three-spoke steering wheel, and higher-end materials.
BYD Denza N8 EV (Source: Autohome)
Ahead of its official launch, the Denza N8 EV was spotted in China undisguised. New images from Autohome show the luxury SUV driving in public, with roof-mounted LiDAR and a sleek, premium look.
Last month, BYD also launched the Denza N8L EV , a slightly longer six-seat version of the current PHEV sold in China.
BYD Denza N8L EV (Source: BYD)
The Denza N8L EV is available in two versions. The N8L EV Premium starts at 299,800 yuan, or about $45,000, while the Flagship model is priced from 329,800 yuan ($49,000).
Both versions use a 130.15 kWh BYD Blade Battery 2.0, providing a CLTC range of up to 596 miles (960 km).
The N8L EV is 5,200 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, or slightly longer than the standard version. It’s about the same size as the current PHEV. The larger SUV features a “208L super-large intelligent electric front trunk.”
Local media suggests BYD will launch the Denza N8 EV on October 26. Check back next week for the full details.

The first response in the RICO case initiated by a group of carriers against giant 3PLs C.H. Robinson and TQL has been filed by the latter, and it has two key arguments.
TQL, in a series of three individual motions filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, is seeking dismissal of the case primarily on the grounds that first, its practices do not rise to the definition of corrupt activity under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO); and two, beyond that, the case is in the wrong court.
A third point is that one of the defendants, IWS Motor Freight, doesn’t have a contractual relationship with TQL.
Arguing about TQL and C.H. Robinson’s behavior (the latter has yet to file a response to the lawsuit) would become moot in the federal court if it accepts TQL’s argument that the venue chosen by the carriers is incorrect.
Let’s do this in Ohio
The core of the TQL argument is that the carrier plaintiffs–Stevens Trucking, Western Flyer Express, Christenson Transportation and E.O.S., in addition to IWS–had agreed in their carrier contracts with TQL “to litigate any dispute with TQL exclusively in the state court located in Clermont County, Ohio.”
Clermont County is a suburb of Cincinnati. TQL is based in that city.
“TQL requests enforcement of those agreements before adjudication of the merits,” the company said in its court filing. “The agreements expressly choose Ohio law.”
In the case of IWS, TQL says it wants that carrier out of the case because it is not based in Texas, and it “had no direct contract with TQL and conducted no business with TQL.”
But it is a second filing by TQL, also submitted Monday, that is the first public record of the operational argument the 3PL might be making in the litigation beyond the question of venue. It is part of a request for a dismissal.
Active docket for TQL TQL had a busy September on the legal front. Besides the RICO case, it did win a victory when it was tossed out as a defendant in a Colorado trial resulting from a fatal incident in that case that involved a truck hired by TQL. It also made its oral arguments in the case involving a carrier named Pink Cheetah , a case that goes to the issue of broker transparency.
No Montgomery impact
And while broker lawsuits now immediately spur thoughts of their impact under Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II , that Supreme Court precedent has no role in the RICO case.
TQL’s primary argument is that the actions and results that the carriers cite as their evidence of a conspiracy among the two big brokers is actually “a dispute about Plaintiffs losing freight to a lower bidder, the likely result of their poor business practices.”
“Plaintiffs dress this ordinary commercial setback that they are solely responsible for in the language of racketeering and false advertising because they cannot plead a single TQL act that caused a single lost account,” the company says in its summary of its motion to dismiss.
TQL’s action tries to separate itself from C.H. Robinson. It says that many of the specific lost accounts the carriers said they suffered because of the brokers’ actions were lost from their relationship with C.H. Robinson, though at no time in its argument does TQL suggest there was any improper activity by C.H. Robinson.
Weak market doesn’t mean illegal practices
“Low rates, carrier noncompliance and a declining freight market do not establish that TQL committed racketeering or false advertising,” the motion to dismiss said.
The suit filed by the carriers cite several shippers who had utilized their services but no longer did, including Johnson Controls, Kroger and Kraft Heinz. In a sentence of almost perfect legalese, the TQL attorneys scoff at these allegations by saying that “those aggregate losses do not identify which injury was caused by the asserted TQL statutory violation.”
In a less legally-driven passage, TQL says the charges leveled against it “contain many anecdotes cloaked as facts, including allegations generally about the industry or of other brokers’ practices and third-party driver injuries, but none of those are elements of the particularly causes of action asserted against TQL–they are merely rhetoric designed to distract from the absence of factual support.”
The carriers’ allegations, TQL says, are mostly “inferences.”
Carrier complaints about low rates “asset contemporaneous fraudulent intent, but they infer it from the premise that low rates necessarily reveal forced labor or that later carrier noncompliance proves an earlier false promise,” the TQL response says.
There are charges in the carriers’ lawsuit about “allegedly falsified records,” as the TQL response puts it. But the broker says the records were only received by TQL, not created by it, and “receipt of a falsified record does not establish TQL’s knowing participation in its falsification.”
In one paragraph that seeks to sum up TQL’s view of the carriers’ arguments, as well as its own defense, the giant 3PL’s retort is that the way brokers work should be known to the carriers, since most of them have their own brokerage arms themselves.
“Plaintiffs’ market-wide theory moves through several steps: carriers allegedly coerce workers or evade regulation; their costs fall; brokers purchase cheaper capacity; freight prices and shipper benchmarks fall; plaintiffs lose bids or operate at reduced margins,” TQL said. “That narrative does not explain which TQL predicate act directly produced a particular plaintiff’s lost account, margin erosion, or aggregate revenue decline. Moreover, Plaintiffs fail to answer how a broker who is using a motor carrier licensed and approved by the Department of Transportation , amounts to fraud or a statutory violation. This is especially true given that at least half of the plaintiffs are licensed as freight brokers with the FMCSA.”
The third motion for a dismissal filed by TQL is directed specifically at carrier IWX Motor Freight, which as noted TQL sees as separate from the other carriers due to the absence of a contractual arrangement between the two companies.

Fiat Ducato, Opel Movano, Citroen Jumper Diesel Vans Recalled Over Fuel Leak Risk
10 photos
Photo: Citroen
Picture yourself in the shoes of a fleet manager. One of the worst-case scenarios in this role is a van going down mid-route. Fiat, Opel, and Citroen just handed fleet operators a good reason to book workshop time, with Stellantis identifying an increased risk of fire due to a potential fuel leak. Per three distinct KBA filings, the fuel pressure damper in the low-pressure system can leak without warning.
The German watchdog lists three reference numbers for this recall, specifically 17165R for the Fiat Ducato, 17166R for the Opel Movano, and 17167R for the Citroen Jumper. All three reports describe the same defect, which is hardly a surprise given that all three models feature similar underpinnings.
Fiat's share is the largest, covering 2,783 large vans produced between July 14, 2026, and July 31, 2026. The Movano recall covers 655 units, while Citroen is aware of 1,486 potentially affected workhorses. Together they add up to 4,924 vehicles, all 2026 models. Production windows differ slightly, of course.
Most large vans from Stellantis' European subsidiary are produced at the Sevel plant in Italy. Said light commercial vehicle plant builds the Ducato, Movano, and Jumper on a shared architecture that also underpins the Vauxhall-branded Movano, Peugeot Boxer, and the Toyota Proace Max. The Sevel plant opened in 1981 and currently prides itself on a daily capacity of 1,200 vehicles per day.
Certain versions hail from Gliwice in Poland, which builds select body lengths, wheelbases, and specialized variants across the recalled nameplates. Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority hasn't clarified where the recall population was produced.
Photo: Citroen The Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt lists all three campaigns as monitored, which means that it's tracking completion rather than investigating the reported issue. In Germany, the recall population includes 1,271 units of the Ducato, 225 of the Movano, and 451 of the Jumper.
These are all work vehicles, and for a fleet operator, pulling vans off the road for a fuel line replacement costs a lot of money in lost job sites or deliveries. Typical of the KBA, the authority does not say how long the repair takes or whether Stellantis Europe will provide loaners.
Customers can check whether their vans are affected by contacting customer support or the dealer of their liking with the relevant campaign number and vehicle identification number. Neither Stellantis Europe nor the KBA has explained why the fuel pressure damper may leak diesel.
The fuel tank of said vehicles is likely connected to the familiar 2.2-liter turbo diesel four-pot mill that Fiat markets as the MultiJet III. Said engine shouldn't be confused with the older MultiJet II design or the even older Ford-PSA lump.
The KBA material fails to mention whether the recalled vans use the 120-, 140-, 160-, or 180-ps version of the MultiJet III engine. Nevertheless, it does highlight a replacement lower fuel line section, damper included, as the remedy.

Data released by energy officials in India shows that more than half of the country’s coal-fired power units are operating with low stockpiles of fuel, as power demand surges and generation from other resources lags.
The country’s Central Electricity Authority (CEA) on October 19 said 96 coal-fired units have critically low amounts of coal on hand. That’s up from 60 coal-fired units that were running with low fuel stocks a month earlier.
Officials said total stockpiles of coal at the nation’s power stations had dropped by about 5% since the start of October. Hotter-than-normal temperatures, linked to the El Niño weather pattern, were driving up demand for electricity, officials said. The government’s coal ministry earlier this month said it told suppliers to increase shipments of fuel to coal-fired plants.
The CEA said that last month the gap between electricity demand and supply increased to 560-million kilowatt-hours, the highest level since August 2023. Bloomberg on October 19, citing sources familiar with the discussions, reported that government officials will hold off on a proposal that would ask coal-fired power plant operators to import more coal. The report said officials had considered asking operators to mix imported coal with domestic supplies to help increase fuel stockpiles, but higher prices for imported coal and a weaker rupee (India’s official currency) pushed that plan aside.
The Indian government has ordered more than 100 coal-fired power plants to run at full capacity from October 1 until at least the end of the year to help meet higher demand for electricity.
More Investment in Coal
A research group last fall said several areas of India were withdrawing support for renewable energy projects and preparing to invest in more coal-fired power generation. POWER reported that government officials in Uttar Pradesh, the state that is home to much of the country’s population, along with authorities in Assam state had made bids to acquire as much as 7 GW of coal-fired power output that would be delivered in the coming years, according to India Ratings & Research. That agency offers credit rating and research services in that country.
The group said those bids come after more than 17 GW of coal-fired generation capacity was contracted from early 2024 through July of last year.
The electricity agency said daily peak power demand this year has been about 45 GW to 50 GW higher year-over-year, and said lower output from India’s hydropower plants due to less rainfall during the monsoon season has brought the need for thermal power stations to produce more electricity. The CEA said coal-fired power generation in September was up 13.3% for the month year-over-year, while hydro output was off 20% from a year earlier.
Government data shows about 55% of India’s power generation comes from resources other than fossil fuels. Officials have said, though, a lack of battery energy storage to support intermittent renewable energy has meant a greater reliance on coal-fired units across the country.
The International Energy Agency in its Coal Mid-Year Update 2026 published in September said India will see a 4.2% rise in its total coal demand to 1.353-billion tons this year. The agency attributed the rise, which comes after coal demand fell in 2025, is due to higher power demand and oil and gas disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz.

Freightos founder Zvi Schreiber’s campaign to change the company’s leadership is heading to a contested shareholder vote, escalating a dispute over the digital freight-booking platform’s strategy, financial performance and long-term prospects.
The company’s board has agreed to put Schreiber’s proposals to shareholders at its annual general meeting in December, pending confirmation of the meeting date.
Schreiber has submitted three resolutions: one to remove Chairman Udo Lange as a director, another to require annual director elections instead of the current three-year terms, and a nonbinding recommendation to appoint a chairman with experience scaling growth-stage technology companies and refocus the strategy on rapid platform growth. However, Schreiber said Freightos has refused to put the strategy recommendation to a shareholder vote. Freightos did not directly comment on that claim in its response to FreightWaves.
The proposals would have different effects. Freightos is incorporated in the Cayman Islands, and its directors currently serve staggered three-year terms, with different classes standing for election at successive annual general meetings. Schreiber’s special resolution proposes shortening those terms to one year, a change that would require an amendment to the company’s articles of association. Schreiber argues the changes are needed to hold Freightos’ leadership accountable for its performance.
Specifically, he said Lange should take responsibility for the company’s performance, pointing to the gap between Freightos’ share-price performance and the broader market.
“It’s certainly not a personal thing, but the board has gone in the wrong direction and delivered very bad results for shareholders, and the chairman should take responsibility,” Schreiber said.
Schreiber also argued that annual elections would make the board more accountable to shareholders.
“That way, the directors are more answerable to shareholders, and we get to decide every year if we’re pleased with the job they’re doing or not,” he said.
Schreiber founded Freightos in 2012, and agreed to step down as CEO effective Jan. 31, 2026, but decided to resign from the board entirely on Feb. 28. CFO Pablo Pinillos took over as CEO following Schreiber’s departure. Schreiber remains a roughly 6% shareholder.
Schreiber said the main driver of his resignation from the board was the decision to prioritize its Solutions business, which sells software and data products, over its digital booking platform, while also slowing the pace of growth. He argued that the shift was particularly misguided as advances in artificial intelligence threaten to make software products easier to replicate.
“To bet that company on solutions first, just when AI is really threatening it, I thought that was a very bad decision,” Schreiber said.
The campaign followed about three months of correspondence and legal pressure from Schreiber. He said he initially held off on publicly challenging the board to give it time to demonstrate that its strategy would work.
“To launch a public campaign against the board? that needs data,” he said. “So I wanted to give them at least six months to prove themselves.”
Over the past year, Freightos shares have fallen about 78%, compared with a roughly 16% gain for the Nasdaq Composite over the same period, according to Nasdaq’s historical index data. The figures provide context for Schreiber’s criticism of shareholder returns, though they do not by themselves establish the causes of the stock’s performance.
After Freightos reported second-quarter results in August showing revenue growth of 3% year over year and a 4% decline in Solutions revenue, Schreiber said he concluded the strategy was not delivering the results he wanted to see. Schreiber has since launched GrowCRGO, an initiative focused on his campaign for changes at Freightos.
“I’m proud of Freightos and very passionate about it and very sad when I see it not being managed in the way which I think is right,” Schreiber said.
Financial performance underpins the dispute
Freightos operates a digital platform that connects airlines, freight forwarders and shippers to price, book and manage international freight. It also sells software and data products to logistics companies.
The company’s second-quarter results showed contrasting performance between the two businesses.
Freightos reported $7.7 million in revenue for the second quarter of 2026, up 3% from a year earlier. Platform revenue increased 19% to $2.9 million, while Solutions revenue, which includes subscription-based software and data services, fell 4% to $4.8 million.
The recent slowdown followed a stronger 2025, when Freightos’ Solutions revenue grew 27% to $19.6 million. The business generated about 62% of the company’s total revenue that year, compared with 38% from its Platform business.
Freightos remains unprofitable on an adjusted EBITDA basis, reporting a loss of $2 million in the second quarter, an improvement from a loss of $2.9 million a year earlier.
Schreiber argues that the company should focus more heavily on its digital marketplace , which he believes offers greater long-term potential than its software business.
“The two principles which I always supported are to grow as fast as you can, and grow primarily the platform, the transactional business. That is where the future is,” Schreiber said.
AI raises the stakes for Freightos’ strategy
The disagreement also reflects a broader debate about how artificial intelligence could reshape freight technology.
Schreiber argues that AI could make traditional software products easier to replicate, weakening the competitive advantage of companies that primarily sell software. Digital freight marketplaces, by contrast, depend on relationships with carriers, access to capacity and networks connecting participants across the industry.
“AI can write software in minutes, but AI can’t go and negotiate with airlines around the world and build a network,” Schreiber said.
For Freightos, the distinction matters because its business combines a digital booking platform with software and data products sold to logistics companies. AI could help improve pricing and booking workflows, but it could also make it easier for competitors to develop applications for freight forwarders and shippers.
Whether AI ultimately strengthens Freightos’ marketplace advantage or increases competitive pressure on its software business remains an open question.
Freightos’ response and the shareholder vote
Freightos said its board and management team are aware of Schreiber’s communications and shareholder proposals and will evaluate them in accordance with the company’s governing documents and fiduciary responsibilities.
“The Board and management remain fully focused on executing our operational strategy and delivering long-term value for all Freightos shareholders,” the company said in a statement to FreightWaves.
The company did not directly address Schreiber’s criticisms of its growth strategy, shareholder returns or approach to AI.
Why this matters
The dispute highlights a strategic question facing freight technology companies as AI advances: whether long-term value lies in software products or digital marketplaces built around carrier relationships and booking networks. For Freightos, the shareholder vote will also test investor support for its leadership and strategy as the company works to grow revenue and reach profitability.

BYD Is Spicing Up Its UK Offering With Truckman Official Accessories for the Shark Pickup Truck
16 photos
Photo: BYD
BYD bet that cool accessories could boost sales of its Shark pickup trucks in the UK, so it partnered with Truckman to offer approved accessories to its customers. The British accessories specialist will supply a wide range of load bed hardtops, tonneau covers and cross bars. Customers will be able to order them directly from BYD retailers in the UK.
While Europeans are not huge pickup truck fans, they occasionally buy them, either for work or leisure. Surprisingly, most of them are midsize trucks, with the most popular being the Ford Ranger and Toyota Hilux. Compact pickups have not caught traction, with Renault/Dacia selling a truck based on the Duster crossover in very limited quantities.
Unsurprisingly, BYD is also entering the European market with a midsize truck called Shark. The Chinese carmaker just started sales in the UK in September, with plans to expand to EU countries in 2027. And since a pickup truck is not merely a vehicle, but a platform, BYD correctly anticipated that a successful market launch requires a compelling accessory offer.
In the UK, BYD partnered with Truckman to design and build the official accessories for the Shark. The British company has over 40 years of experience in supplying accessories for pickups, so it was a natural choice for BYD. Since British pickup truck owners are just as fond of pimping up their vehicles as those across the Pond, Truckman should significantly boost BYD Shark's capabilities and appeal.
Hardtops are among the most popular truck accessories, and the new partnership doesn't disappoint. The Grand Hardtop option is color-coded to match the vehicle. It comes with pop-out windows, rear window heating, and remote central locking. This provides a weatherproof cover for the truck's bed without compromising on looks.
Photo: BYD The M-Series hardtop provides a more rugged alternative, which sports a powder-coated finish. Gull-wing side windows make it easy to load and unload from both the sides and the rear of the truck. This is also more versatile than the Grand Hardtop, providing multiple mounting options for a wide range of accessories.
Two Truckman tonneau covers will be offered, one with a manually retractable cover and the other electrically actuated. The latter can be remotely opened and closed via a smartphone app. Both covers feature an IP56 weather resistance rating and a T-slot system to fit optional cargo bars. These include the Heavy Duty Black Cross Bars, which can withstand a dynamic load of 200kg and a static load of 360kg.
A cool accessory for those who want easy access to tools, camping equipment, and appliances in the bed is the DragMat. This slides in and out of the bed and can handle over 100 kg (220 lb) of cargo. It can also provide extra protection against scuffs and scratches for the load bed, if that's something a truck owner should worry about.
The BYD Shark is an off-road-capable plug-in hybrid that gives its more seasoned rivals a run for their money. It uses a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine and a pair of electric motors, one at the front and the other at the rear. These are powered by a 32.2 kWh battery, one of the largest in the segment. Total power reaches 430 hp, developed by the two electric motors, with the petrol engine acting as a generator.

Officials in Virginia have voted to approve a plan for a massive natural gas-fired power plant in the central part of the state near the James River.
Supervisors in Cumberland County, about an hour west of the state capital Richmond, on October 20 voted 3-1 in support of the Cumberland Energy Center, a 3,000-MW gas-fired station planned by Dominion Energy. The vote Tuesday came after hours of public comment about the facility. The local planning commission in August had recommended approval of a conditional use permit required for the project.
“We look forward to continuing to engage with the community as we move forward with this very vital project, not only to our customers in providing reliable power but also to the Cumberland community,” said Jeremy Slayton, a Dominion Energy spokesperson, in a statement. The project still needs an air permit from the state Department of Environmental Quality and approval from the Virginia State Corporation Commission.
Dominion has said the Cumberland Energy Center would use two, 2-on-1 combined cycle gas-fired units to generate about 3 GW of baseload power. The utility said power station is sited on about 150 acres off Duncan Store Road in Cumberland County. Dominion has said it is targeting 2029 to begin construction of the project.
Natural Gas-Fueled Buildout
The utility earlier this year projected that over the next two decades it would have to build as many as six natural gas-fired power plants, in addition to more renewable energy projects, in order to meet the growing demand for electricity in its territory. State officials already this year have approved Dominion’s proposal to build five solar and battery storage projects, and approved 10 power purchase agreements, totaling as much as 1 GW of power generation capacity.
Dominion has not given an official estimated cost for the Cumberland station, but the utility has said it will be a “multi-billion-dollar project.” Slayton earlier this year confirmed the Cumberland Energy Center would cost more than Dominion’s Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center , a 944-MW gas-fired power plant that regulators approved last year. The Chesterfield plant, with a price tag of $1.47 billion, is being built on the site of the Chesterfield Power Station, a power plant whose last operating coal-fired units were retired in 2023. The new gas-fired plant is being built near the existing gas-fired Units 7 and 8 (with 446 MW of generation capacity) at Chesterfield.
The region in Virginia is home to several power generation facilities and planned energy projects. James River Industrial Park, a site about 7 miles south of the James River Industrial Center near Interstate 95, in late 2024 was chosen as the location for what could be the world’s first nuclear fusion power plant. Commonwealth Fusion Systems in December 2024 said the company would build a 400-MW fusion facility on a 100-acre site at the industrial park.
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

Dodge Durango Owners Who Paid For Taillamp Repairs or Replacements Can Now File for Reimbursement
66 photos
Photo: Dodge
One of the most recognizable parts of the Durango can be found out back. Referred to as the racetrack taillamp by its maker, this full-width assembly is known to go dark a few LEDs at a time. Dodge finally made the reported problem its own, confirming that coverage on the rear lights now runs five years from the vehicle's in-service date. Unlimited miles, of course, but there's a catch.
The extension applies to certain 2018 through 2024 model year Durango sport utility vehicles, covering taillights that fail to illuminate or do so only partially. As it happens, the rear lighting units used by Dodge for those model years of the Durango may allow water to slip past the gaskets and seals. If that moisture pools where it has no business doing so, the LED circuit ultimately corrodes.
Given that diodes live on a sealed board, nobody in their right mind is willing to swap in a dead segment. The whole assembly has to go, and it's an expensive replacement. Dodge indirectly acknowledged the problem through a couple of technical service bulletins, namely TSBs from March 2020 and June 2021, meaning that Dodge is aware of the problem for at least six years now.
Owners and lessees have been paying close to $2,000 for replacement assemblies for many years now. For example, a December 2025 complaint filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration carries an $1,800 dealer quote (labor included). The five-year extension announced today pays some of that back.
Anyone who already covered such replacements out of pocket can file claims with Dodge using a dedicated website. Alternatively, customers and lessees can mail in the reimbursement form that comes with the customer notification letter. Reimbursements naturally require some documentation, so customers have to dig out appropriate proof of payment before trying to get their money back.
Photo: Dodge The website Dodge uses for Durango taillight claims is fcarecallreimbursement.com, and that's a bit curious. Is the Dodge brand using the same portal FCA US LLC, a.k.a. Stellantis North America, uses for recall refunds? It sure is, and it's now attached to a campaign that is not described as a recall even though partial or a lack of rear illumination increases the risk of a crash.
After some digging, yours truly discovered that a class action has been asking the courts for exactly what this warranty extension is not. Filed in the US District Court for the District of Delaware, the Cranstoun et al. v. FCA US LLC federal class-action lawsuit seeks either a court-ordered recall or full financial compensation for affected customers.
The class action covers 2014 through 2023 models, and one owner's complaint to the NHTSA describes a near-rear-end collision in 2019. Worse still, the same owner also described repeated police stops for their dead rear lights. Looking at the bigger picture, the Auburn Hills-based automaker may have decided on a customer satisfaction program because repairing it if the condition actually shows up is much cheaper than repairing potentially affected Durangos wholesale.
Matt McAlear, the chief executive officer of Dodge, frames the program as standing behind Durango owners. The racetrack taillights help the Durango stand out from other three-row people haulers, and McAlear credits customer feedback for this extension.
What now? If the rear lights work as intended in full, nothing. Only if segments go dark or glow faintly, then call your preferred dealer and let the extension handle the invoice. Durangos past the five-year window get six months of coverage from the notification date.

1970 Buick GSX 455 in Saturn Yellow Is a Rare 4-Speed Luxury Muscle Car, Paint Job Took 17 Months
50 photos
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy
Imagine your family doctor showing up for a house call in 1970 driving a radioactive banana with a hood-mounted tachometer, black racing stripes, and a Hurst 4-speed stick shift. Wrap all that in a cloud of smoke, because 510 lb-ft of torque would tend to turn black rubber into white fog. Ask any Hemi owner from back then what was it like to look at that car from behind, and watch it pull away. That’s what the GSX was all about – elegant manners of a tire iron adorned with a silk pompon.
No, not GTX; one letter before that – T is right after S in the alphabet, and the GTX was behind the GSX on the drag strip. And in cubic inches. And in torque. And in swagger. That glorious contradiction is the exact vibe radiating from the 1970 Buick GSX 455 featured by automotive journalist Jim Campisano on his Muscle Car Campy YouTube channel, where owner Timothy Blanch shows off one of Flint’s loudest velvet-gloved street brawlers ever.
Blanch is a die-hard Bowtie loyalist who has owned his 1969 Chevrolet Camaro for 45 years and kept a Chevrolet Chevelle for 12 years before crossing into Buick territory. After 43 years of work, Tim Blanch retired, and found himself a new hobby – restoring the most luxurious muscle car ever made.
A friend pulled this GSX out of New England 15 years ago, and Blanch traded his Chevelle to acquire it in 2016. He stripped the car, shipped the shell to Pennsylvania for a 17-month paint job, and reassembled it himself. I don’t know what they did in that paint booth for almost a year and a half, but its looks could stop Saturn’s moons in their orbit, that’s how yellow it is. Saturn Yellow, to be precise. (and please note that Saturn has 293 confirmed natural satellites, but NASA’s still counting).
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Even after finishing the wrenching, Blanch waited a full year to score the proper reproduction wheels before letting Campisano film the ride. Wearing the blinding Saturn Yellow paint, identified by the exclusive QQ trim tag code that General Motors reserved solely for the 1970 GSX, this coupe radiates attitude. Inside, it skips air conditioning for a Sonoramic AM radio, a short consolette, and a padded GSX tilt wheel measuring one inch less in diameter than the regular Buick GS 455. “Regular.”
As both men point out while rowing the Muncie M20 wide-ratio 4-speed gearbox, the Buick cabin looks way more upscale and chrome-trimmed than any period Chevelle SS. That country-club swagger paired with street-brawler punch goes right back to the birth of the Gran Sport moniker. Buick launched the Skylark Gran Sport midway through the 1965 model year on the intermediate A-body platform to give Pontiac’s hot-selling GTO a proper migraine.
Because General Motors brass banned intermediate cars from carrying engines reserved for the full-size series (usually larger than 400 cubic inches), Buick pulled a cheeky corporate sleight of hand for 1965 and 1966. Engineers dropped in their venerable 401-cubic-inch Nailhead V8, slapped a Wildcat 445 sticker on the air cleaner, and called it a 400-incher.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy It churned out 325 horsepower at 4,400 rpm and a stump-pulling, tire-frying 445 pound-feet of torque at just 2,800 rpm. In 1967, Buick shortened the badge to GS 400 and retired the Nailhead for a modern 400-cubic-inch V8 rated at 340 horsepower and 440 pound-feet of torque, joined by a 260-horsepower GS 340 sibling.
A sleeker restyle in 1968 brought the 280-horsepower GS 350 alongside the GS 400, before the 455-cubic-inch behemoth arrived in 1970. The original rear-wheel-drive V8 Gran Sport bloodline finally bowed out after the 1975 model year.
When General Motors lifted its displacement cap for 1970, Buick unleashed the ultimate showroom magnet: the GSX, short for Gran Sport Experimental. Introduced in March 1970 to battle the Pontiac GTO Judge and Oldsmobile 4-4-2 W-30, the GSX package added chin and decklid spoilers, black stripes, front disc brakes, heavy-duty suspension, and wide tires. The $1,196 option, soon discounted to $1,100, stacked onto the $3,283 GS 455 hardtop base price.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Under that black-striped hood lurked a lightweight 455-cubic-inch V8 that weighed roughly 150 pounds less than a Chrysler 426 Hemi or Chevrolet 454. Even in standard trim like Blanch’s car, with a 10.0:1 compression ratio and a four-barrel carburetor, the 455 delivered 350 horsepower at 4,600 rpm and an earth-spinning 510 pound-feet of torque at 2,800 rpm. That torque figure stood as an American production car record for 33 years.
Buyers who ticked the Stage 1 box got a 10.5:1 compression ratio, bigger valves, a wilder camshaft, and a reworked Rochester Quadrajet carburetor. Buick advertised it at 360 horsepower at 4,600 rpm and 510 pound-feet of torque to fool insurers, though real output topped 400 horsepower. Period testers clocked the base 455 GSX from 0 to 60 mph in 6.5 seconds, running the quarter-mile in 14.28 seconds at 100.5 mph.
With a top speed reaching 129 mph in Car Life testing, the big Buick had serious legs, while Motor Trend rocketed a 1970 Stage 1 from 0 to 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and through the quarter-mile in a blistering 13.38 seconds at 105.5 mph. Despite those superhero numbers, buyers were scarce across its three-year run from 1970 to 1972, with Buick assembling just 846 GSX coupes in total. There were no other body styles available, by the way.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy The debut 1970 model year accounted for 678 of those cars, split by color into 491 Saturn Yellow examples and 187 Apollo White ones. By engine, 400 buyers upgraded to the Stage 1 455, while 278 kept the standard 350-horsepower 455. Across all 678 cars, 479 carried the optional Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 3-speed automatic transmission, leaving only 199 factory examples equipped with the 4-speed manual gearbox and Hurst floor shifter.
Digging deeper into 1970 records, those 400 Stage 1 cars included 118 4-speeds (78 yellow and 40 white) and 282 automatics (214 yellow and 68 white). Meanwhile, the 278 standard 455 coupes featured 197 automatics (142 yellow and 55 white) and just 81 4-speeds, split into 57 in Saturn Yellow like Blanch’s gem and 24 in Apollo White, though some archives tally 79 base manuals and 120 Stage 1 sticks.
By 1971, tightening emissions dropped compression to 8.5:1, trimming ratings to 315 horsepower and 450 pound-feet on the base 455, and 345 horsepower with 460 pound-feet on the Stage 1, while Buick also opened the GSX package to additional factory colors and the 260-horsepower 350-cubic-inch V8. Production tumbled to 124 cars for 1971, which enthusiast registries estimate at roughly 62 Stage 1s, 30 standard 455s, and 32 small-block 350 coupes.
In 1972, a switch to SAE net ratings adjusted the 455 to 250 horsepower and the Stage 1 to 270 horsepower, and only 44 final-year GSXs left the factory. Those 44 cars comprised 16 350-cubic-inch models (15 automatics, and a single 4-speed), 4 base 455s (3 automatics, 1 4-speed), and 24 Stage 1s (22 automatics, a pair of 4-speeds).

BMW is preparing to introduce its first three-row electric SUV. With its official debut coming up, the iX7 was spotted testing, offering a sneak peek at the full-size luxury SUV.
BMW iX7 spotted ahead of 2027 debut
The iX7 is the electric version of BMW’s largest and most luxurious SUV. Although BMW has yet to announce it officially, disguised prototypes were recently caught testing at the Nürburgring in Germany.
After the iX3 and iX5, the iX7 is the next BMW SUV in line to debut with its Neue Klasse technology and design.
Like the iX5, BMW’s three-row electric SUV will retain a more traditional style than the full-on Neue Klasse EVs, such as the iX3.

While it’s still covered, the image posted on Reddit shows the grille appears much wider and chunkier than the slim, upright updated Kidney Grille design on the iX3. It also features split headlights, similar to the current X7, rather than the wider headlights on Neue Klasse models.
The iX7 also drops the conventional pull-style door handles in favor of small handles located on the vehicle’s pillar.
BMW iX7 caught testing at the Nürburgring with seven seats few have asked for by u/gaukmotors in MotorBuzz
BMW will reveal details closer to its debut, expected in mid-2027. Like the smaller iX5 60 xDrive, the iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. The iX5’s AWD setup delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, which BMW said enables it to hit 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.
Powered by a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the iX5 will offer up to 435 miles of range. It will also use an 800V electrical system for fast charging.

Tesla says it now has 1.74 million active “Full Self-Driving” subscriptions, up 67% from a year ago. A footnote in its Q3 2026 shareholder letter explains how it gets there: the metric follows “our 2025 CEO Performance Award” and “includes both upfront payment and monthly subscriptions.”
So owners who bought FSD outright, some of them years ago, count as subscribers. That matters because 10 million active FSD subscriptions is one of the milestones Elon Musk has to hit to earn his 2025 pay package. It also matters because hundred of thousands of those FSD “subscribers” were sold unsupervised self-driving, which Tesla has yet to deliver.
How Tesla counts FSD subscriptions
Here’s what Tesla has reported under that definition:
Quarter | Active FSD subscriptions
Q3 2025 | 1.04 million
Q4 2025 | 1.10 million
Q1 2026 | 1.28 million
Q2 2026 | 1.48 million
Q3 2026 | 1.74 million
Tesla stopped selling FSD as a one-time purchase on February 14, 2026. New customers can only get it as a subscription, at $99 a month in the US. But everyone who paid upfront before that, at prices that reached $15,000, stays in the count as long as the car is active. The only exclusion is free trials.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
We flagged this in April when Tesla reported 1.28 million. Six months later, Tesla still doesn’t say how many of the 1.74 million actually pay every month.
The same approach shows up elsewhere in the letter. Tesla’s “cumulative deliveries” figure, now 10.2 million, also counts “any unsupervised Robotaxis placed into commercial operation,” again to match the pay package, which has a 20 million vehicle milestone.
The 75% attach rate
Tesla also says more than 75% of new deliveries in North America included FSD subscriptions in Q3, “a nearly twenty percentage point sequential increase.” It says it believes “FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available.”
That’s a big number, and Tesla doesn’t define it. The letter doesn’t say whether it counts subscriptions started at delivery with an introductory offer, or how many of those buyers are still paying after a few months. The active-subscription metric excludes free trials, but Tesla doesn’t say the same about the attach rate.
The road to 10 million
Musk’s 2025 award has 12 tranches. Each requires a market cap milestone and one operational milestone. The operational list includes 20 million vehicles delivered, 10 million active FSD subscriptions, 1 million Optimus robots, 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation, and adjusted EBITDA targets. As of June 30, Tesla considered only one of them probable : 20 million deliveries.
Tesla added 260,000 net FSD subscriptions in Q3, its best quarter yet. At that pace, it would take about eight years to reach 10 million. At the pace of the last 12 months, about 700,000 a year, it would take closer to 12. The award runs until 2035.
Electrek’s Take
Counting people who bought FSD outright isn’t wrong on its own. Those cars do have the software. The problem is calling them “subscriptions” and presenting the total as proof of momentum, when the definition was written for Musk’s pay package and not for investors trying to understand the business.
Also, you promised unsupervised self-driving to many of those “subscribers.” Hardly a win to count them now in a “supervised” service with no end in sight for the supervision.
This is now Tesla’s headline software metric. The board wrote the definition, Musk’s compensation depends on it, and the company won’t say how many people pay $99 a month. Tesla obviously knows that number.
The attach rate is the more interesting claim, if it holds up. A 75% take rate on a $99-a-month product would be a real business. So show us the retention: how many North American buyers who started a subscription in Q2 are still paying today?

source_document.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman speak as they arrive during the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Leaders’ Summit at The Ritz-Carlton on May 14, 2025 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has built his rule on security and prosperity, the simple concept that a modernized Saudi Arabia would also be a safer and more prosperous one. However, that promise is now under unprecedented strain.
Repeated missile and drone attacks have targeted Saudi airfields, threatened the Kingdom’s oil-processing hub at Abqaiq and forced the shutdown of the East-West pipeline — the strategic lifeline intended to bypass Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The latest attacks on Riyadh’s international airport have brought the war to the Kingdom’s capital, further exposing the limits of its defenses and the vulnerability of its economic ambitions.
The Prince still retains firm control over the security establishment, faces no organized domestic opposition capable of challenging his rule and commands substantial financial resources. But his unprecedented concentration of power has made him the indispensable center of the Saudi system, while also making the system’s fortunes increasingly inseparable from his own.
It is against this backdrop that Washington is moving forward with a nuclear cooperation agreement that could allow uranium enrichment on Saudi soil. The debate has focused on safeguards, proliferation risks and what the United States might receive in return.
But the Kingdom’s mounting security crisis raises a more fundamental question: What happens when Washington transfers nuclear capabilities designed to last half a century to a political system whose future cannot be confidently predicted? And what can the US Congress do to ensure there are safeguards in place should Saudi policy, by choice or not, change in the coming years?
The agreement signed in July 2026 opens a pathway to enriching uranium on Saudi soil. It provides for a two-year study of commercial enrichment, initially limited to uranium enriched to 5 percent, with additional review before any move toward 20 percent. Under the proposed arrangement, a facility would reportedly be operated by American companies using a “black box” model intended to prevent Saudi personnel from accessing sensitive centrifuge technology. However, the agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which provides more intrusive off-site verification measures.
The central problem, however, is not simply whether the proposed safeguards are sufficient. It is the assumption that the political circumstances under which nuclear capabilities are transferred will remain sufficiently stable over the decades in which those capabilities exist.
The current war demonstrates why such an assumption is risky. Despite enormous investments in military modernization, Saudi Arabia has struggled to protect vital infrastructure against comparatively inexpensive missiles and drones. Its efforts to diversify export routes have also revealed their limitations. The East-West pipeline, designed to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, became a target itself. Meanwhile, Houthi advances along the Red Sea have threatened another critical maritime passage, Bab el-Mandeb.
The consequences extend beyond immediate military damage. Saudi Arabia’s economic transformation depends on attracting foreign investment, expanding tourism, developing new industries and convincing international businesses that the Kingdom is a safe and predictable environment. Repeated attacks on airports, energy facilities and transportation networks undermine precisely that perception.
External military pressure, damage to critical infrastructure, mounting war costs and declining economic confidence could become far more destabilizing if compounded by a future succession crisis or fractures within the ruling elite or security establishment. Concentration of power can strengthen a regime while its center remains secure, but it can also increase vulnerability if that center comes under strain.
None of this means regime change is imminent; that is the wrong standard for nuclear policy even if it were. Washington does not need to predict the fall of the House of Saud. It needs to recognize that no one can confidently predict the character of the Saudi political order over the lifetime of a nuclear energy program.
The problem becomes considerably more serious when uranium enrichment is involved. Enrichment is not simply another component of civilian nuclear energy. It is a strategic capability that can provide a foundation for a future weapons program. A black-box arrangement may restrict access to centrifuge designs, but it cannot entirely prevent the accumulation of expertise, trained personnel and institutional knowledge. Once these capabilities exist, they cannot simply be recalled if relations with Washington deteriorate or Saudi Arabia’s political order changes.
Saudi leaders have also been unusually explicit about the strategic significance of nuclear capabilities. In 2018, Mohammed bin Salman declared that if Iran developed a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow suit. More recently, the Kingdom’s defense agreement with nuclear-armed Pakistan introduced an additional nuclear dimension into Riyadh’s security relationships, even if subsequent Pakistani statements qualified the extent of those commitments.
Iran provides an uncomfortable historical warning. The US helped establish Iran’s civilian nuclear program when the Shah was one of Washington’s closest regional partners. Under Atoms for Peace, Washington supplied Iran’s first research reactor and helped train Iranian nuclear scientists.
Then the political system changed.
The Islamic Republic’s present enrichment capabilities were not simply inherited from the American-supported program, of course. But the larger lesson remains: nuclear institutions, expertise and ambitions can survive the political order under which they were created. Technology can outlive the strategic assumptions that justified its transfer.
Congress should therefore examine more than proliferation safeguards. It should also conduct a political durability assessment. Who would control enrichment capabilities during a future succession crisis? Could nuclear facilities be secured during prolonged regional conflict? What happens if relations with Washington deteriorate? And what political forces might ultimately inherit the infrastructure and expertise the US helped establish?
This does not mean Saudi Arabia should be denied civilian nuclear energy because its political future is uncertain. It means that the more sensitive and enduring the technology being transferred, the less policymakers should rely on confidence in today’s leadership as a substitute for durable safeguards and long-term strategic planning.
Mohammed bin Salman may successfully navigate the present crisis. But nuclear policy must account for the possibility that the Kingdom’s political character will change substantially over time.
The US is considering a decision whose consequences could endure well beyond Mohammed bin Salman and perhaps beyond the present Saudi political order itself. Nuclear reactors can operate for 50 years or more. The infrastructure, expertise and sensitive fuel-cycle capabilities associated with them can outlive governments and even political systems. An agreement concluded with Mohammed bin Salman today could therefore shape the capabilities available to Saudi leaders in the 2050s, 2060s and beyond.
The relevant question is not simply whether Washington trusts Saudi Arabia with sensitive nuclear technology today. It is whether Washington is prepared to trust the Saudi Arabia that might inherit it tomorrow.
Yoel Guzansky heads the Institute for National Security Studies’ Gulf Studies program, served on Israel’s National Security Council (2005-2010), and co-authored Fraternal Enemies: Israel and the Gulf Monarchies (2020).
Henry Sokolski runs the Nonproliferation Policy Education Center in Arlington, Virginia, served as the Pentagon’s deputy for nonproliferation policy (1989-1993) and authored Underestimated: Our Not So Peaceful Nuclear Future (2019).
