Trucking shouldn’t just offer somebody a seat. It should offer them a future, better skills, better opportunities, and more money and choices. That was the premise Werner Enterprises Senior Director of Driver Recruiting Ben Pile brought to his recent appearance on Brake Check with host Charles Gracey.
Pile has spent 23 years in driver recruiting, and his experience has ranged across nearly every pressure point carriers face in attracting and keeping drivers today: equipment quality, trust, the make-or-break first 90 days, and the different needs of rookie and veteran drivers. According to Pile, recruiting only gets a carrier in the door, and it’s everything that happens after that determines whether a driver stays.
What separates Werner’s genuine career path from a shallow recruiting pitch, Pile says, is the sheer range of directions a driver can take.
“There’s over 400 different driving opportunities here,” Pile said, citing multiple regions, local routes, dedicated lanes, and team driving as just a starting point. Drivers can also move into leadership roles mentoring the next generation, become driver ambassadors or Road Team Captains, or get behind the wheel of one of Werner’s Operation Freedom trucks. Being a Marine Corps veteran himself, Pile says that program is near and dear to his heart.
But opportunity only matters if the basics are covered first, and for Pile that starts with equipment. “Our tractor age is two and a half years. Not a lot of carriers can say that,” he said, adding that Werner’s trailer fleet averages five years old. “That equipment is the baseline for your job. If you don’t have a good, safe piece of equipment, then you’re not rolling down the road making the money that you deserve.”
Given Werner’s scale, Pile hears from a wide cross-section of drivers who’ve left other carriers, and he said the reasons tend to cluster around two issues. “Most of it is equipment and not being treated with respect,” he said. “That’s what I hear the most.”
Gracey pushed further, noting that recruiters across the industry often get an unfair reputation for overpromising, much of which stems from a disconnect between what recruiting sells and what the operation looks like in practice. Pile said Werner works to close that gap by holding recruiters to the same standard drivers are promised.
“We are constantly monitoring driver profiles that the recruiters are selling, pay structures, things like that, giving those operation leaders a chance to look at those descriptions of accounts to make sure it matches the expectation of the fleet,” Pile said. “The last thing I want is recruiters selling something that isn’t reality. So we do very good diligence on that every single quarter, if not weekly, at all times.”
That diligence, Pile said, is what builds the trust drivers need to buy in.
“They’re trusting us, coming on board, knowing that we have the opportunity that we described for them — being honest with them about the home time, the pay, the equipment, and the opportunities that we have here,” Pile said.
If recruiting gets a driver in the seat, Gracey argued, retention is won or lost in the first 90 days, and that’s where the spotlight shifts from recruiter to operation. Pile said one of the most common mistakes carriers make is expecting new drivers to hit full productivity immediately.
“Some carriers have expectations that drivers are going to be very productive from day one,” Pile said. “That’s not always the case. They have to learn the ropes of that particular account. It does take time. We mentor, and we’re very patient with our drivers. We provide a lot of coaching along the way on how they can get better, how they can earn that income.”
When expectations and reality don’t line up right away, Pile said Werner treats it as a conversation rather than a dead end. “Maybe I came here with my expectation being X and Y, and now it’s A and B. Let’s figure it out. Let’s see what other opportunities are available if this isn’t a good fit,” he said. “I’d hate for you to leave because of this kind of circumstance. Let’s try to find out what’s a better fit for you within the organization.”
Simply asking drivers for feedback already puts a carrier ahead of much of the industry, but what a company does with that feedback matters even more.
Pile said Werner leans on direct, recurring outreach. “We want the feedback — reaching out to them, having calls, just checking in,” he said. “How’s it going? Tell me about your account. What’s good? What’s bad? I think getting that real feedback from the drivers firsthand is vital in your organization.”
Follow-through, in Pile’s view, is what separates a listening exercise from real retention work. “As long as you get follow-up from them, I think they’re more engaged in what you’re doing day to day than they would be if they make a complaint and no one follows up with them. It falls on deaf ears,” he said. “Actions speak louder than words when it comes to that. You’re not going to have every answer, of course, but as long as you’re explaining the why and the reasoning behind it, I think a lot of people will understand that.”
Pile was clear that new and experienced drivers require very different retention strategies. For drivers fresh out of driving school, he said the approach is hands-on and constant.
“It’s coaching all the time. It’s following up with them more often than you probably will with an experienced driver. It’s finding them a mentor on the fleet, someone they can lean on,” Pile said, noting that new drivers need a resource as they encounter unfamiliar situations for the first time.
Veteran drivers need something different. “It’s been there, done that,” Pile said. “But everybody needs a mentor in their life” — which is why Werner pairs experienced drivers with senior peers as well. When he’s talking to a driver with 20 years of experience weighing a move, Pile said he starts with a question: “What are you looking for in a carrier? What are you looking for in a driving position?” From there, he said, it’s about matching that individual to the right pay, home time, equipment, and location. “It’s all about that individual and what the right fit is for them.”
Werner’s size, Pile argued, is itself a retention tool. The carrier owns Roadmaster Driving School, giving it a pipeline into training itself, and earlier this year acquired FirstFleet, Inc., which brought a wave of local driving opportunities into the fold. Beyond the truck, Werner offers advancement into safety roles, terminal management, and its Road Team Captain program, along with niche opportunities like hazmat-endorsed freight.
Pile pushed back on some of the stigma around hazmat hauling: “There are a lot of myths about hazmat. It’s not all about hauling dangerous nuclear waste. In Werner’s case, it’s often something as simple as a load of paint. You’re just more marketable as a driver if you’re able to haul hazmat.”
When a driver’s needs change mid-career, Pile said Werner’s internal career center exists specifically to find a new fit without losing the driver altogether. “That is a group of folks that is dedicated strictly to filling drivers’ needs internally,” he said. If an over-the-road driver decides they need to be home more, “I’ll get you on a list, and you could be on that fleet in the next, I don’t know, 30 to 90 days — and you could be home weekly, if not daily, depending on where you’re at in the country.”
With driver acquisition costs ranging anywhere from $7,000 to $15,000 depending on the carrier, Gracey raised a pointed question: at what point does retention, not recruiting, become the real priority?
Pile didn’t disagree. “Two-way communication is the only real defense against turnover,” he said. “I just think there’s so much pay and so many different opportunities that it can be ridiculous to leave a carrier just to go across the street and start over again. Stay at a carrier. Get stability with them. Grow your career path and build on what you’ve done.”

Son Drives His Dad's Ultra-Rare $1.7 Million Supercar, Has Over 800 Horsepower and No Windshield
12 photos
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
His father has a garage of dream cars. Of all of them, his son would choose the $1.7 million McLaren Elva. "It is the best car I've ever driven, by a lot," he says, although he finds the hood-mounted mirror ridiculous and the suspension terrible.
McLaren originally announced a production run of 399 cars. Shortly after launch, the British house slashed the production by 150. Former CEO Mike Flewitt explained that the brand received immediate feedback from its collector base. Customers spending north of $1.7 million complained that a 399-unit run was unworthy of an Ultimate Series hypercar.
The cap was lowered by customer demand to provide greater exclusivity. Later in 2020, McLaren quietly announced the final reduction, capping the total build run at no more than 149 examples due to restrictions and factory shutdowns caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. At the time, all of them were already spoken for.
The one that Aidan's father bought is car number 10 of the 149 that saw the light of day. Aidan says he talked to Max Verstappen, and the four-time Formula One champion had already sold it. I did a bit of digging, and Max has never owned an Elva . The one who had one was Fernando Alonso.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube The Spaniard owned car number 114. It was auctioned off by Bonhams on November 25, 2023, in Abu Dhabi, with only 3 miles (5 kilometers) on the clock, but it failed to reach the $2.5 million reserve, and Alonso retained ownership of the car. He quietly sold it shortly after for an undisclosed sum.
However, Aidan's father is by no means planning to sell his Elva. He is actually a McLaren collector and plans to stay that way. He has a 720S Spider and a 750S parked in his garage and a W1 on the way. While the Elva started at $1.7 million when new, the W1 is a $2.1 million deal before fees and options.
The plug-in hybrid hypercar comes with 1,258 horsepower (1,275 metric horsepower) and 988 pound-feet (1,340 Newton meters) of torque. This time, production remains limited to 399 units, with no plans for the British company to lower that number.
Aidan gets to drive them all for one reason. His father likes boats more than he likes cars. So the 720S Spider , the 750S, and the Elva take turns, and he says that the latter is the best car he has ever driven, by a lot. That's because it handles like a go-kart, it turns like a go-kart, and it grips back like a go-kart.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube For the money, the buyer got a roofless, windowless, and even windshield-less speedster. McLaren did offer a fixed physical glass windshield as a factory option for markets like the United States, but the upright glass altered the aerodynamics of the vehicle, so many of the customers went for the complete wind-in-your-hair experience.
The Elva is powered by a 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8, which pushes out 804 horsepower (815 metric horsepower) and 590 pound-feet (800 Newton meters) of torque. That is what pushes it from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 2.7 seconds and to a top speed of 203 mph (326 kph).
The V8 has to push forward only 2,531 pounds (1,148 kilograms). The ultralight architecture integrates a carbon fiber monocoque, while the full outer body comprises three main carbon fiber panels: front clamshell, the rear clamshell, and a massive single-piece wrap-around upper body element that flows into the cabin.
The vehicle lacks a roof, side windows, the windshield, the rear glass, the glove box, and the audio speakers, and even the seats are unique, lightweight carbon shells. In the meantime, upgrades such as the 3D-printed titanium exhaust system and titanium brake calipers save significant weight.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube In a conversation wth TJ Lamb from Magnacars, Aidan says the hood-mounted mirror is useless, but it looks awesome. There is something that he dislikes about the cabin. It lacks a temperature gauge, something that all his other McLarens do have. However, none of them are this light.
To protect the occupants from being battered and buffeted by the wind, McLaren came up with a world-first technology called the Active Air Management System (AAMS). Air is sucked into the front splitter and directed out of a hood outlet, while the carbon fiber deflector automatically rises 5.9 inches (150 millimeters) from the hood, which redirects air around the car to create what McLaren calls the "Bubble of Calm."
The Elva came with a pair of bespoke helmets developed in partnership with Bell Racing, but with a single storage space under the rear carbon-fiber tonneau cover for one helmet. Aidan says he doesn't wear it because it makes him look like a cartoon character. The interior panel of the door is painted just like the exterior, and there is no glovebox.
Two seats, a steering wheel, and two screens, that's all you get on board the Elva. It is obvious that storage space has never been a priority when designing the model. Well, the McLaren Elva is definitely not about storage space, but about the wind-in-your-hair experience.

Toyota Recalls 105,794 Land Cruiser Hybrids in the US for a Fuel Leak It Cannot Explain
225 photos
Photo: Toyota
Toyota Motor North America has a problem it spent around two years trying to understand. It still cannot explain that problem, and that makes this recall all the more interesting. As it happens, a retaining clip on a fuel tube connection can lift, separate the joint, and let gasoline leak. Per TMNA, up to 105,794 examples of the Land Cruiser are being recalled over this concern.
26V673 is the NHTSA campaign number, whereas Toyota refers to it as 26TA23. Covering model years 2024 through 2027 and production dates from November 29, 2023, to October 1, 2026, the 250-series Land Cruiser population is enormous. Truth be told, it appears to cover all US-market vehicles produced through October 1, 2026.
Toyota's US subsidiary cannot estimate how many examples of the Prado carry the defect because it never found the root cause behind those iffy clips. The resin fuel tube on the fuel tank connects to a main metal fuel tube feeding the turbocharged inline-four mill up front. If the retaining clip on that connector lifts, the joint comes apart, and that's bad news if there's an ignition source nearby.
Toyota Motor North America started hearing about this in 2024. Dealer technicians found the retainer clip lifted or missing on reported vehicles, reseating the connector or swapping the resin tube under warranty. The Japanese manufacturer then went looking for a manufacturing-related root cause, but came up empty.
CCTV footage from the factory showed the clip perfectly seated at the time of assembly, and production records showed no process deviation or rework. Even supplier sampling data confirmed dimensions within Toyota's specifications. FTS Co. is the supplier in question, and its investigation involved recovered tubes from the US and overseas markets.
Photo: Toyota The supplier's investigation found markings on the connectors consistent with the tube being pulled apart while the retainer clip sat in an unlocked state, pointing to the clip being lifted after the subject population left the factory. TMNA then tried to break the connection, performing pull tests on newly manufactured tubes with properly seated clips.
Said testing showed the connector housing failing before any disconnect. Vibration and pressure tests followed suit, along with vibration and pressure runs. All failed to separate a properly installed joint. Given the aforementioned, Toyota 's safety boffins then drove Prados through standing water at various depths and speeds.
Only when the clip was left deliberately unseated did the connection let go. This scenario leads to a joint failure, which eventually results in the fuel pump shutting off while driving. When that happens, the Land Cruiser 250-series hybrid drops into electric mode with reduced power.
At the beginning of October 2026, the automaker was aware of 23 field technical reports and 64 warranty claims in the US market. The fix comes in the form of a supplemental clamp to keep the joint from separating. If the dealer inspection calls for it, the resin fuel tube may be replaced at no charge to affected customers.
Dealers were notified on October 14, while customer letters are expected to be mailed between November 29 and December 13. In the meantime, the most practical move is to get in touch with your dealer or perform a VIN check on Toyota's consumer website.

Tesla’s energy business deployed more batteries in Q3 2026 but brought in less money. Energy generation and storage revenue fell 16% year-over-year to $2.88 billion, even though storage deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh.
Tesla’s shareholder letter blames the drop “partially” on “tariff-related customer refunds.” It doesn’t say how much it refunded, to which customers, or why it was accounted for as reduced revenue.
Tesla Energy’s Q3 2026 numbers
Here’s how the segment has moved over the last five quarters, based on Tesla’s reported results:
Quarter | Storage deployed | Energy revenue | Energy gross margin
Q3 2025 | 12.5 GWh | $3.42B | 31.4%
Q4 2025 | 14.2 GWh | $3.84B | 28.6%
Q1 2026 | 8.8 GWh | $2.41B | 39.5%
Q2 2026 | 13.5 GWh | $3.14B | 20.4%
Q3 2026 | 13.7 GWh | $2.88B | 33.1%
Gross margin bounced back to 33.1% from 20.4% in Q2. But energy gross profit still fell to $954 million from $1.07 billion a year ago, and Tesla listed “lower Energy Generation and Storage gross profit” among the reasons its operating income fell 56% .

Year-to-date, Tesla has deployed 36 GWh, up 11% from 32.5 GWh over the same period of 2025. Energy revenue is down 6% to $8.43 billion. Deployments also came in well short of the roughly 15.9 GWh analysts expected for Q3.
Tariffs keep moving Tesla’s energy numbers
This isn’t the first time tariffs have shown up in the energy segment this year. In Q1, Tesla listed “energy one-time benefits related to tariffs” among the drivers of its profit improvement, and energy gross margin hit 39.5%. We questioned those levers at the time , and Tesla never put a dollar figure on the energy portion.
Now money is flowing the other way. Tesla doesn’t explain the refunds, but the most likely reading is that some storage customers paid tariff-related charges that Tesla no longer owed after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February. That’s a guess, though, and the letter leaves investors to make it.
Building its own LFP cells
The rest of the energy news in the letter is about getting tariffs out of the supply chain. Megafactory Texas started production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai. Tesla also shipped its first Megapacks built entirely with its own LFP cells from Nevada, where it has 7 GWh of cell capacity in early ramp.
Tesla says storage demand is at its “highest-ever order rate and backlog,” driven by data centers that need power faster than the grid can deliver it. One of those customers is Musk’s own: xAI, now part of SpaceX, bought another $269 million of Megapacks this year, after $430 million of purchases from Tesla in 2025.
Electrek’s Take
Energy was supposed to be the steady part of Tesla while the car business stalled. This year it’s been anything but steady: a 39.5% margin in Q1, 20.4% in Q2, 33.1% in Q3, and revenue down even as deployments rise. A lot of that noise is tariffs, and Tesla keeps describing them without quantifying them.
Now, if Tesla is really reimbursing customers for tariffs, it’s a good thing. Many companies getting tariffs refund are pocketing them. So kudos to Tesla.
With that said, the company’s own CEO is responsible for getting elected the clown who installed those illegal tariffs in the first place. So…

A blast at Fortuna Mining's Lindero gold mine in Argentina's high-Andes. Credit: Henry Lazenby
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 21, 2026
Fortuna Mining (TSX: FVI; NYSE: FSM) has drilled gold beneath the planned bottom of its Lindero open pit in Argentina’s high-Andes, strengthening its case for adding reserves at the operating mine.
Hole LDH-272 returned 350 metres grading 0.96 gram gold per tonne from surface, including 98 metres averaging 0.91 gram below the pit design, the company reported Tuesday. Lindero lies about 260 km from Salta, the provincial capital, in Argentina’s high-altitude Puna region.
“Broad intersections strengthen the case for including below-pit material in a revised pit and reserve estimate,” National Bank analyst Mohamed Sidibé wrote in a Tuesday note.
Lindero accounts for 32% of National Bank’s forecast company-wide production this year and 28% of its estimated net asset value. The bank’s operating model includes only existing reserves, although its valuation already assigns some value to resources outside the mine plan, Sidibé said.
Fortuna aims to determine how much deeper material can enter an expanded pit and revised mining schedule, with updated resource and reserve estimates planned for release in the first quarter of next year.
Fortuna shares fell about 1.4% to $14.35 by mid-Wednesday in Toronto, valuing the company at $4.27 billion. They’ve traded between $10.78 and $18.99 over the past year.
Deeper targets
The company expanded this year’s diamond drilling program to 8,534 metres in 31 holes from an initial 6,000 metres after encouraging early results. Work focused on improving confidence in inferred resources beneath the southern portion of the planned pit, where earlier drilling had identified higher-grade gold.
A second hole, LDH-259, cut 236 metres averaging 0.85 gram from surface, including 94 metres grading 0.66 gram below the pit design. Both below-pit intervals exceed the 0.54-gram average grade of Lindero’s existing reserves, although drilling alone doesn’t establish that the material can be mined economically.
The reported intervals are downhole lengths. Fortuna hasn’t defined true widths because mineralization forms a roughly circular body associated with a porphyry intrusion.
Crews collected samples to check expected gold recoveries from material scheduled for mining over the next two years. Fortuna aims to finish updating its geological model and pit design by year-end, incorporating the new drilling and indicated resources already identified beneath the pit.
Operating base
Lindero held 64.4 million tonnes of proven and probable reserves grading 0.54 gram gold, containing about 1.1 million oz., at Dec. 31, 2025. Fortuna documentation puts the remaining reserve life at nine years as of that date.
The heap-leach operation, which The Northern Miner visited for an April 2025 report, poured its first gold in October 2020.
Production rose 25% from the second quarter to 26,024 oz. in the three months through September as improved equipment availability lifted crushing and stacking rates, Fortuna said. Lindero’s nine-month output reached 68,398 oz., with Fortuna maintaining the mine’s annual guidance of 92,000 to 102,000 ounces.
Fortuna also operates the Séguéla gold mine in Côte d’Ivoire and the Caylloma silver-lead-zinc mine in Peru. It expects to produce between 281,000 and 305,000 gold-equivalent oz. this year.
